title: Deploy Apache Web Server on RHEL 10
description: Categorise and sequence the steps to deploy a secure Apache HTTP server on a fresh RHEL 10 instance, from subscription registration through SELinux hardening.
scenario: A fresh RHEL 10 server needs Apache deployed and secured. Drag each step into the correct deployment phase (Prepare, then Install, then Configure, then Harden) and arrange the steps in the right order within each phase.

steps.text: Register the system with Red Hat Subscription Manager
Patch the base OS before installing new packages
Install the Apache HTTP server package (httpd)
Install mod_ssl for TLS support
Set the ServerName directive in httpd.conf
Create the document root index.html
Enable and start the httpd service
Allow HTTP and HTTPS through firewalld (permanent)
Reload firewall rules
Restore correct SELinux file context on the web root

explanation:
Apache deployment on RHEL 10 follows four phases. Within a phase, some steps have real ordering dependencies and some do not.

**1. Prepare** (get the host ready before installing anything)
1. Register with `subscription-manager` so `dnf` can reach the correct repos
2. Patch the base OS with `dnf update`

**2. Install** (put packages on disk, do not configure them yet)
1. Install `httpd`
2. Install `mod_ssl` (the SSL module plugs into an already-installed `httpd`, so `httpd` must exist first)

**3. Configure**
- Set the `ServerName` directive in `/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf`
- Create `/var/www/html/index.html`
- *(either order above is fine)*
- Run `systemctl enable --now httpd` last; the service must boot against a valid config and real content

**4. Harden**
- Open firewall ports with `firewall-cmd --add-service` (must come before reload)
- Run `firewall-cmd --reload`; reload only applies rules already added
- Run `restorecon -Rv /var/www/html`; independent of the firewall steps, but belongs in Harden rather than Configure because it enforces SELinux policy on files written during configuration
learningOutcomes: Sequence RHEL system administration tasks across operational phases
Understand Apache deployment prerequisites and configuration order
Apply firewalld and SELinux hardening after service configuration
realWorldValue: Deploying web servers in the correct order prevents both security gaps and service failures. RHEL environments require subscription management, SELinux context management, and firewalld rules. Skipping or misordering any phase results in a non-functional or insecure server.

title: Configure NFS Server on RHEL 10
description: Build the correct command sequence to configure an NFS server on RHEL 10. Exclude dangerous distractors and arrange the real commands in the right order, then watch them run.
scenario: A RHEL 10 server must export /exports/data to the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet over NFS. Drag the correct commands into the queue in the right order. Three of the listed commands are distractors that should never be run in production.

commands.errorOutput: nfs-utils must be installed first. All other steps depend on it.
Install nfs-utils first before creating the export directory.
/etc/exports does not exist yet, or the export directory has not been created. Install nfs-utils and create the directory first.
Cannot start nfs-server before the package is installed and /etc/exports is configured.
exportfs needs the NFS server running and /etc/exports configured. Enable nfs-server first.
FirewallD: --reload must be run after --add-service, not before.
firewall-cmd --reload must come after --add-service so there are rules to reload.
RPC: Program not registered. The NFS server must be running and exports active before showmount can query them.
DISTRACTOR: Disabling SELinux enforcement violates production security policy. Use setsebool or restorecon to manage permissions instead.
DISTRACTOR: Stopping firewalld instead of adding service rules exposes the entire server to the network. Always add specific service rules.
DISTRACTOR: World-writable export permissions are a serious security risk. Use specific UIDs, GIDs, or ACLs to control access.

explanation:
The NFS setup has two independent chains that can interleave, as long as internal order within each chain is respected.

**NFS chain** (strict order):
1. `dnf install -y nfs-utils` (everything else depends on this package)
2. `mkdir -p /exports/data` (create the export directory before referencing it in `/etc/exports`)
3. `echo ... >> /etc/exports` (configure the export after the directory exists)
4. `systemctl enable --now nfs-server` (start the server after `/etc/exports` is configured)
5. `exportfs -arv` (re-read `/etc/exports` after the server is running)
6. `showmount -e localhost` (verify last, once the server is active and exports are live)

**Firewall chain** (can run at any point, as long as `--reload` follows `--add-service`):
1. `firewall-cmd --add-service={nfs,mountd,rpc-bind} --permanent`
2. `firewall-cmd --reload`

**Distractors to avoid:**
- `setenforce 0`: disabling `SELinux` enforcement violates production security policy; use `setsebool` or `restorecon` instead
- `systemctl stop firewalld`: exposes the server to the network; add specific service rules instead
- `chmod 777 /exports/data`: world-writable exports are a serious security risk; use UIDs, GIDs, or ACLs
learningOutcomes: Configure a complete NFS server stack on RHEL 10 in the correct order
Identify and exclude dangerous sysadmin antipatterns from a command sequence
Understand which firewalld services are required for NFS (nfs, mountd, rpc-bind)
realWorldValue: NFS is a core component of RHEL infrastructure for shared storage. Getting the configuration order wrong, or including dangerous shortcuts, leads to inaccessible shares, SELinux AVC denials, or network-exposed data. This lab mirrors the exact workflow you would follow when setting up NFS on a production Red Hat system.

title: Install and run nginx on RHEL 10
description: Type each command into the terminal to install nginx, enable it on boot, and inspect its logs. Flags can appear in any order. Use --help when you get stuck.
scenario: A fresh RHEL 10 host needs `nginx` installed, started, set to launch on boot, and verified through the journal. Complete the three commands in order. Each command accepts its flags in any order, and `<command> --help` lists options including distractors that are not needed for this task.

steps.hint: You need the `install` subcommand, the package name, and a flag that answers yes to every prompt.

requirements.description: install                        install a package
-y, --assumeyes                assume yes to all prompts
<package>                      name of the package to install

distractors.description: --refresh                      set metadata as expired before running the command
--allowerasing                 allow erasing of installed packages to resolve dependencies
-q, --quiet                    suppress command output

steps.task: Enable `nginx` to start on boot AND start it right now, using a single `systemctl` invocation.
steps.hint: One flag tells systemctl to also start the unit immediately, on top of enabling it.

requirements.description: enable                         enable one or more unit files
--now                          when used with enable, also start the unit right now
<unit>                         the unit to operate on

distractors.description: --user                         manage user services instead of system services
--runtime                      make changes only until next reboot (not persistent)
--no-block                     do not wait for the operation to finish

steps.task: Using `journalctl`, show the last 50 log lines for the `nginx` unit.
steps.hint: You need two flag/value pairs: one to filter by unit, one to limit the number of lines.

requirements.description: -u, --unit=UNIT                show entries from the specified unit
-n, --lines=N                  show the last N entries

distractors.description: -f, --follow                   follow the journal, printing new entries as they arrive
-r, --reverse                  show the newest entries first
--since=DATE                   show entries on or newer than the specified date

steps.successOutput:
-- Logs begin at Mon 2026-04-13 09:12:04 UTC --
systemd[1]: Starting The nginx HTTP and reverse proxy server...
nginx[2031]: nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok
nginx[2031]: nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful
systemd[1]: Started The nginx HTTP and reverse proxy server.

explanation:
Three commands cover the full install, run, verify loop on RHEL 10.

**1. `dnf install -y nginx`**
- `install` is the dnf subcommand that installs a package
- `-y` (or `--assumeyes`) skips the interactive confirmation prompt, important in scripts and one-shot labs
- `nginx` is the package name
- Distractors like `--refresh` (force-refresh metadata), `--allowerasing` (allow conflicting packages to be removed), and `-q` (quiet) are valid dnf flags, they just are not needed here

**2. `systemctl enable --now nginx`**
- `enable` creates the boot-time symlink so the unit starts on every boot
- `--now` is the shortcut that also starts the unit immediately, avoiding a separate `systemctl start` call
- Distractors: `--user` operates on user units (wrong scope), `--runtime` makes a non-persistent change (defeats the point of enabling on boot), `--no-block` just affects how systemctl waits

**3. `journalctl -u nginx -n 50`**
- `-u nginx` filters the journal to the `nginx` unit
- `-n 50` limits output to the last 50 entries
- Long-form equivalents (`--unit=nginx`, `--lines=50`) work the same way
- Distractors: `-f` follows new entries (blocks the terminal), `-r` reverses order, `--since=DATE` is a time filter, none of which are required by the task

**Flag order does not matter.** `systemctl --now enable nginx` and `systemctl enable nginx --now` are both accepted, because systemctl (and most RHEL CLIs) parse flags positionally by name, not by position in the command line.
learningOutcomes: Install, enable, and verify a service on RHEL 10 from the command line
Use `--help` to identify the right flags and distinguish them from distractors
Combine `enable --now` and flag-value pairs like `-u unit` and `-n count`
realWorldValue: Every RHCSA candidate and RHEL admin runs this loop constantly: install a package, enable-and-start the service, check the journal. Getting the flags right from memory, with or without `--help`, is the difference between confident command-line work and paging through documentation for every task.

title: Provision an LVM Logical Volume on RHEL 10
description: Categorise and sequence the steps to provision a new LVM logical volume on RHEL 10, from partitioning a raw disk through to a persistent XFS mount.
scenario: A second disk `/dev/sdb` has been added to the RHEL 10 host. Provision it as an LVM logical volume, format it XFS, and mount it persistently at `/mnt/data`. Drag each step into the correct phase and arrange any order-dependent steps within each phase.

steps.text: Identify available disks and their current partition layout
Create a GPT partition table on /dev/sdb
Create a primary partition spanning the full disk
Initialise the partition as an LVM physical volume
Create volume group vg_data from the physical volume
Allocate a 1 GB logical volume named lv_data
Format the logical volume with the XFS filesystem
Create the /mnt/data mount point directory
Add a persistent fstab entry for lv_data
Mount all filesystems from fstab and verify the new mount

explanation:
LVM provisioning follows four distinct phases. Each phase has hard prerequisites on the previous one.

**1. Prepare** (get the disk ready before LVM can use it)
1. `lsblk` confirms which device to use and checks for existing partitions
2. `parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt` writes a GPT partition table; must run before any partitions can be created
3. `parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary 1MiB 100%` carves out a partition; the 1 MiB start offset avoids alignment warnings

**2. Create** (build the LVM stack on the partition)
1. `pvcreate /dev/sdb1` stamps LVM metadata onto the partition; the partition must exist first
2. `vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb1` creates the volume group from the physical volume
3. `lvcreate -L 1G -n lv_data vg_data` carves out a 1 GB logical volume; the volume group must exist first

**3. Format** (prepare the logical volume for use)
- `mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_data` writes the XFS filesystem; must come after `lvcreate`
- `mkdir -p /mnt/data` creates the mount point; independent of the mkfs step, but both must exist before mounting

**4. Mount** (make the volume available and persistent)
1. The `/etc/fstab` entry must be written after both the filesystem and the mount point exist
2. `mount -a` reads `/etc/fstab` and mounts everything listed, which validates the entry immediately without rebooting
learningOutcomes: Sequence LVM provisioning across the correct operational phases (Prepare, Create, Format, Mount)
Understand why each LVM layer (`pvcreate`, `vgcreate`, `lvcreate`) must be created in strict order
Distinguish between filesystem formatting tasks and OS-level persistence via `/etc/fstab`
realWorldValue: LVM is the default storage abstraction on RHEL and is tested directly on the EX200 exam. Provisioning a logical volume from a raw disk is a core hands-on task. Running `mkfs` before `lvcreate`, or writing the `fstab` entry before formatting, are common mistakes that leave the host in a broken state.

title: Configure the chrony NTP Client on RHEL 10
description: Build the correct command sequence to install and verify the chrony NTP client on RHEL 10. Exclude deprecated and destructive distractors and arrange the real commands in the right order.
scenario: A RHEL 10 host needs accurate time synchronisation configured using `chrony`. Drag the correct commands into the queue in the right order. Three of the listed commands are distractors that must not be run in production.

commands.errorOutput: `chrony` must be installed before any other step. Install the package first.
`chrony` must be installed before `chronyd` can be enabled. Run `dnf install -y chrony` first.
`chronyd` must be running before `chronyc` can communicate with it. Enable and start the service first.
`chronyd` must be running before `chronyc sources` can query its NTP sources. Enable and start the service first.
DISTRACTOR: `ntpdate` is deprecated and removed on RHEL 10. It also conflicts with a running `chronyd`. Use `chronyc makestep` for a one-shot time adjustment instead.
DISTRACTOR: Stopping `chronyd` removes time synchronisation rather than configuring it. Never stop the daemon as part of an NTP setup workflow.
DISTRACTOR: Setting NTP to false disables time synchronisation entirely. The correct approach is to ensure `chronyd` is enabled and running.

explanation:
`chrony` is the NTP implementation shipped with RHEL 10 and is tested on EX200 under Skill 7.1.4 (Configure time service clients).

**Setup chain** (strict order):
1. `dnf install -y chrony` installs the `chrony` package, which provides both `chronyd` (the daemon) and `chronyc` (the control tool)
2. `systemctl enable --now chronyd` enables the daemon on boot and starts it immediately in one step

**Verification chain** (either order, both required; both depend on the service being active):
- `chronyc makestep` tells the running `chronyd` to slew the clock immediately rather than waiting for gradual correction
- `chronyc sources` lists the configured NTP sources and their reachability

**Distractors to avoid:**
- `ntpdate pool.ntp.org`: the `ntpdate` command is deprecated and removed on RHEL 10; it also conflicts with a running `chronyd`
- `systemctl stop chronyd`: stops the daemon and removes time synchronisation
- `timedatectl set-ntp false`: instructs systemd to disable NTP synchronisation entirely
learningOutcomes: Install and start the `chrony` NTP client on RHEL 10 using `dnf` and `systemctl`
Verify time synchronisation using `chronyc sources` and `chronyc makestep`
Identify deprecated (`ntpdate`) and destructive commands to exclude from an NTP workflow
realWorldValue: Accurate time is a dependency for Kerberos authentication, TLS certificate validation, log correlation, and scheduled tasks. RHCSA candidates are expected to configure `chrony` from scratch. The EX200 exam frequently tests whether you can distinguish `chronyd` configuration from deprecated `ntp` tooling and destructive one-liners.

title: Create and Harden a User Account on RHEL 10
description: Type each command to create a developer account with the correct home directory and shell, add the user to a supplementary group without overwriting existing memberships, then enforce a 90-day password policy. Use --help to identify the right flags.
scenario: A new developer named `webdev` needs an account on a RHEL 10 host. Create the account with a home directory and `/bin/bash` as the login shell, add them to the `developers` supplementary group without removing any existing group memberships, then set a 90-day maximum password age. Flags can appear in any order. Use `<command> --help` to explore options.

steps.task: Create user `webdev` with a home directory and `/bin/bash` as the login shell.
steps.hint: You need `useradd` with a flag to create the home directory and a flag-value pair to set the shell.

requirements.description: -m, --create-home             create the user's home directory
-s, --shell SHELL             login shell for the new account
<username>                    name of the new user account

distractors.description: -r, --system                  create a system account (no home directory, no password aging)
-u, --uid UID                 force a specific UID for the new account
-e, --expiredate DATE         set the account expiry date (YYYY-MM-DD)

steps.task: Add `webdev` to the `developers` supplementary group without removing their existing group memberships.
steps.hint: Without a specific append flag, `-G` replaces all supplementary groups instead of adding to them. Both flags are required.

requirements.description: -a, --append                  append to the supplementary groups; always combine with -G
-G, --groups GROUPS           supplementary group list to add or replace
<username>                    account to modify

distractors.description: -g, --gid GROUP               change the primary group (not a supplementary group)
-d, --home HOME               change the user's home directory path
-l, --login LOGIN             change the user's login name

steps.task: Set a maximum password age of 90 days for `webdev` using `chage`.
steps.hint: One flag-value pair specifies the maximum number of days between password changes. Watch out for the lowercase variant which controls something different.

requirements.description: -M, --maxdays DAYS            maximum number of days between password changes
<username>                    account to configure

distractors.description: -m, --mindays DAYS            minimum number of days between password changes
-W, --warndays DAYS           days of warning before password expiry
-I, --inactive DAYS           days after expiry before the account is locked

explanation:
User account management covers EX200 Domain 9 and involves three separate tools, each with distinct flags.

**Step 1: `useradd -m -s /bin/bash webdev`**
- `-m` (or `--create-home`) creates `/home/webdev`; without it the user has no home directory and interactive login may fail
- `-s /bin/bash` sets the login shell; the default on minimal RHEL installs is often `/sbin/nologin`, which blocks interactive logins
- Distractors: `-r` creates a system account with no home and no password aging; `-u` forces a specific UID; `-e` sets an account expiry date (separate from password aging policy)

**Step 2: `usermod -a -G developers webdev`**
- `-G developers` sets the supplementary group list; without `-a`, this replaces all existing supplementary groups and can silently lock the user out of groups they already belong to
- `-a` (append) must always accompany `-G` when the intent is to add to groups, not replace them
- Distractor: `-g` changes the primary group (GID in `/etc/passwd`), not the supplementary list

**Step 3: `chage -M 90 webdev`**
- `chage` manages password aging non-interactively and is the standard tool for this on RHEL
- `-M 90` (uppercase) sets the maximum days between password changes to 90
- `-m` (lowercase) sets the minimum days; easy to confuse with `-M` and a common exam trap
- `-W` sets warning days; `-I` sets the inactive lock period; neither controls the maximum age
learningOutcomes: Create a user account with `useradd -m -s` to set home directory and login shell
Safely append a supplementary group with `usermod -a -G` without overwriting existing memberships
Set password aging policy non-interactively with `chage -M`
realWorldValue: EX200 Domain 9 tests user and group management hands-on. The `-a` flag omission with `usermod -G` is a classic RHCSA mistake that silently removes users from all other groups. Knowing `chage -M` versus `chage -m` by flag case is exactly the kind of detail the exam probes under time pressure.

title: Configure SSH Key-Based Authentication on RHEL 10
description: Sequence the steps to replace SSH password authentication with key-based authentication across client and server, from keypair generation through sshd hardening and verification.
scenario: A RHEL 10 bastion host is migrating from password to key-only SSH authentication. Drag each step into the correct phase (Client Prep, then Distribute, then Server Harden, then Verify) and arrange any order-dependent steps within each phase.

steps.text: Generate an ed25519 keypair on the client
Tighten ~/.ssh directory permissions on the client
Copy the public key to the server account
Ensure authorized_keys is 0600 on the server
Disable password authentication in sshd_config
Disable direct root login in sshd_config
Validate sshd config syntax before reloading
Reload sshd to apply the hardened config
Open a new session authenticating with the key
Confirm password authentication is now rejected

explanation:
Key-based SSH cutover has a strict order across four phases because each phase depends on artefacts produced by the previous one.

**1. Client Prep**
1. `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` produces `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (private) and `id_ed25519.pub` (public). ed25519 is the modern default — smaller and faster than RSA for equivalent strength.
2. `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` tightens the directory; SSH refuses to use keys if the parent directory is world- or group-writable.

**2. Distribute**
1. `ssh-copy-id` appends the public key to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server and sets correct permissions. Runs over the existing (password) session — so it must come *before* password auth is disabled.
2. `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` is a defensive belt-and-braces step; sshd rejects authorized_keys with loose permissions.

**3. Server Harden** (never skip the config validation)
- Disable `PasswordAuthentication` and `PermitRootLogin` — either order is fine, they are independent edits.
- `sshd -t` validates syntax *before* reloading. Reloading a broken sshd can leave you locked out.
- `systemctl reload sshd` re-reads config without dropping existing sessions — safer than `restart`.

**4. Verify** (prove the new config works before closing your current session)
- A successful key-based login confirms the distribute phase.
- Rejecting a forced password attempt (`-o PubkeyAuthentication=no`) confirms the harden phase. Both must pass before you log out of the password session that got you in.
learningOutcomes: Generate an ed25519 keypair and deploy it with `ssh-copy-id`
Edit `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` safely and validate syntax with `sshd -t` before reloading
Separate client-side, server-side, and verification work when cutting over authentication methods
realWorldValue: Every RHEL admin is expected to configure key-based SSH — it is explicitly tested in EX200 Skill 10.1.3. Disabling password authentication before proving the key works is one of the most common RHCSA lockouts; this phased approach mirrors the safe cutover every production runbook follows.

title: Resolve SELinux Denials for a Custom Web Root on RHEL 10
description: Diagnose and remediate an Apache 403 caused by SELinux on a non-default document root, covering file context relabelling, port labels, and boolean tuning.
scenario: Apache has been reconfigured to serve `/srv/web` on port 8080, but clients receive a 403 and httpd refuses to bind to the port. SELinux is Enforcing. Drag each step into the correct phase (Investigate, then Relabel, then Policy, then Verify) and order the steps within each phase.

steps.text: Confirm SELinux is in Enforcing mode
Review recent AVC denials in the audit log
Inspect current SELinux context on the new web root
Install the policy management tooling
Define the persistent httpd_sys_content_t mapping
Apply the new file context recursively
Label TCP port 8080 as an http_port_t
Persistently enable the httpd_enable_homedirs boolean
Reload httpd to pick up the new policy
Confirm a request to :8080 now succeeds

explanation:
SELinux troubleshooting almost always follows investigate → relabel → policy → verify. Skipping the investigate phase leads to guess-driven changes that damage policy rather than fix it.

**1. Investigate**
- `getenforce` confirms the mode: if it says `Permissive`, nothing you are about to do is required for function; it is still good hygiene.
- `ausearch -m avc -ts recent` extracts the exact Access Vector Cache denials from the audit log, including source/target contexts and the port or path involved.
- `ls -Z /srv/web` shows the current label. A freshly created directory under `/srv` typically inherits `var_t`, which is not readable by `httpd_t`.

**2. Relabel** (make the change persistent)
- `policycoreutils-python-utils` provides `semanage`; on a minimal install it is not present.
- `semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?'` registers the mapping in the policy database, so relabels survive a future `restorecon` or `relabel on reboot`.
- `restorecon -Rv /srv/web` applies the mapping to files on disk. Always follow an `fcontext` change with `restorecon` — the mapping alone does not relabel existing files.

**3. Policy**
- `semanage port` labels a non-standard port so `httpd_t` is allowed to bind to it. Without this, `httpd` refuses to start on 8080 regardless of file context.
- `setsebool -P` toggles a policy boolean persistently. `-P` is critical: without it, the change reverts on reboot.

**4. Verify**
- Reload httpd so it re-reads labels and port rules.
- `curl -I` confirms the service now responds on the new port without a 403. Verify with a real request, not just absence of errors in the log.
learningOutcomes: Triage SELinux denials with `getenforce`, `ausearch`, and `ls -Z` before changing policy
Apply persistent file context with `semanage fcontext` + `restorecon`, and port labels with `semanage port`
Toggle policy booleans persistently with `setsebool -P` and verify end-to-end with `curl`
realWorldValue: Most RHCSA SELinux failures are not about switching SELinux off — they are about knowing which surface to fix: context, port, or boolean. EX200 Domain 10 tests each of these directly. Reaching for `setenforce 0` hides the problem and is a deduction on the exam and a terminable offence in production.

title: Configure a Static IPv4 Address with nmcli on RHEL 10
description: Build the correct command sequence to configure a static IPv4 address, gateway, DNS, and hostname on RHEL 10 using nmcli. Exclude commands that rely on deprecated network-scripts tooling.
scenario: A RHEL 10 host named `web01` needs a static IPv4 address of `192.168.10.50/24`, a gateway of `192.168.10.1`, and DNS servers `9.9.9.9` and `1.1.1.1` on interface `ens160`. Drag the correct commands into the queue in the right order. Three of the listed commands are distractors from the deprecated network-scripts era and must not be used on RHEL 10.

commands.successOutput:
NAME     UUID                                  TYPE      DEVICE
ens160   9c6f...                               ethernet  ens160
commands.errorOutput: Inspect the current NetworkManager connections first so you know which profile name to modify.
Confirm the connection name with `nmcli connection show` before modifying it.
Confirm the connection name with `nmcli connection show` before modifying it.
Confirm the connection name with `nmcli connection show` before modifying it.

commands.command: nmcli connection modify ens160 ipv4.method manual
commands.errorOutput: Set the addresses, gateway, and DNS before switching the method to manual, otherwise NetworkManager has nothing to apply.
Set the hostname at any point in the workflow — it is independent of the interface configuration.
Activate the connection only after method is set to manual and the address/gateway/DNS attributes are all configured.

commands.successOutput:
2: ens160: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 ...
    inet 192.168.10.50/24 brd 192.168.10.255 scope global ens160
commands.errorOutput: The connection must be active before `ip addr show` reflects the new address. Bring the connection up first.
DISTRACTOR: The `network.service` unit from legacy network-scripts does not exist on RHEL 10. NetworkManager is the sole network provider; use `nmcli connection up`.
DISTRACTOR: Hand-editing `ifcfg-*` files bypasses NetworkManager and is deprecated on RHEL 10 — the network-scripts package is no longer installed by default and keyfile profiles are preferred.
DISTRACTOR: `ifup`/`ifdown` are provided by the legacy network-scripts package which is not installed on RHEL 10. Use `nmcli connection up` instead.

explanation:
Static IPv4 configuration on RHEL 10 is done exclusively through NetworkManager — `network-scripts` is gone and `network.service` no longer exists.

**Inspect first**
- `nmcli connection show` lists profiles. The *profile name* (e.g. `ens160`) is what `nmcli modify` takes, not necessarily the device name.

**Attribute chain** (all four must be set; order of 2/3/4 is free, method must come last):
1. `ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.50/24` — address plus prefix in CIDR form
2. `ipv4.gateway 192.168.10.1`
3. `ipv4.dns "9.9.9.9 1.1.1.1"` — multiple servers space-separated inside one quoted argument
4. `ipv4.method manual` — switches the profile from DHCP to static. Do this last so the previous attributes already exist when NetworkManager applies the method.

**Activate + verify**
- `nmcli connection up ens160` applies the change immediately. Skipping this leaves the new config in the profile but not on the interface.
- `ip -4 addr show ens160` is the authoritative check that the kernel has the address.
- `hostnamectl set-hostname` is fully independent and can run at any point — it does not touch NetworkManager.

**Distractors to avoid:**
- `systemctl restart network` targets a unit that does not exist on RHEL 10.
- Writing `ifcfg-*` files directly bypasses NetworkManager and the `network-scripts` package is no longer shipped.
- `ifup`/`ifdown` belong to the same deprecated package.
learningOutcomes: Configure static IPv4 addresses, gateway, and DNS on RHEL 10 using `nmcli connection modify`
Activate a NetworkManager profile and verify with `ip -4 addr show`
Recognise deprecated network-scripts tooling (`ifup`, `ifcfg-*`, `systemctl restart network`) and avoid it on RHEL 9/10
realWorldValue: RHEL 10 ships NetworkManager as the only supported network stack. EX200 Domain 8 tests this configuration directly and the exam graders expect nmcli — reaching for ifcfg files or `systemctl restart network` will not function at all on a fresh RHEL 10 install.

title: Inspect and Preserve systemd Journals on RHEL 10
description: Build the correct command sequence to investigate httpd errors and enable persistent journal storage on RHEL 10. Exclude destructive commands that would erase diagnostic evidence.
scenario: A RHEL 10 host has a flaky `httpd` service and journals are being lost on reboot because persistence was never enabled. Drag the correct commands into the queue in the right order to investigate the current failure and then make the journal persistent. Three of the listed commands are distractors that would erase evidence or disable logging.

commands.successOutput:
IDX BOOT ID                          FIRST ENTRY                 LAST ENTRY
   0 5f3a...                          Mon 2026-04-13 09:12:04 UTC Mon 2026-04-19 14:02:11 UTC
commands.errorOutput: Start by inspecting the boot history so you know which boot contains the failure you want to investigate.

commands.successOutput: Apr 19 13:51:02 rhel10 httpd[2041]: (13)Permission denied: AH00072: make_sock: could not bind to address [::]:8080
commands.errorOutput: List the boots first so it is clear which boot the errors you are about to read come from.
Create the persistent journal directory before restarting systemd-journald so the daemon finds it and starts writing there.
Create `/var/log/journal` first. Restarting systemd-journald without the directory leaves journals in `/run` (volatile) as before.
Only useful once persistent journals exist under `/var/log/journal`. Enable persistence first.
DISTRACTOR: Deleting `/var/log/journal` destroys every persistent journal on the host. Never use this to 'clean up' logs — use `journalctl --vacuum-size` or `--vacuum-time` with a sensible bound.
DISTRACTOR: A 1-second vacuum threshold erases virtually every journal entry including the evidence you just came here to read. Use realistic retention such as `--vacuum-time=2weeks`.
DISTRACTOR: Disabling systemd-journald stops all journal collection. The goal is persistence, not disabling logging.

explanation:
The journal workflow has two independent chains that share one prerequisite (being on the right host) but otherwise do not overlap.

**Investigation chain** (strict order):
1. `journalctl --list-boots` — shows the index and boot IDs. Knowing *which* boot you are reading from is a precondition to any meaningful triage.
2. `journalctl -b -u httpd -p err` — filter to the current boot (`-b`), the `httpd` unit (`-u`), and priority error or worse (`-p err`). The error priority filter is what surfaces the real signal out of noisy access logs.

**Persistence chain** (strict order):
1. `mkdir -p /var/log/journal` — the mere existence of this directory is the switch that tells systemd-journald to write persistently. No config edit is required on RHEL 10.
2. `systemctl restart systemd-journald` — picks up the new directory. Without the restart, the daemon keeps writing to `/run/log/journal` (volatile).
3. `journalctl --verify` — confirms the persistent files are well-formed and not truncated.

**Distractors to avoid:**
- `rm -rf /var/log/journal` — destroys all persistent journals. Use `--vacuum-size` or `--vacuum-time` for controlled cleanup.
- `journalctl --vacuum-time=1s` — a 1-second retention is effectively the same as deletion. Pick something realistic like `2weeks` or `500M`.
- `systemctl disable --now systemd-journald` — disables the entire journal subsystem, which is the opposite of what you want.
learningOutcomes: Filter `journalctl` output by boot (`-b`), unit (`-u`), and priority (`-p err`)
Enable persistent journals by creating `/var/log/journal` and restarting `systemd-journald`
Distinguish controlled journal cleanup (`--vacuum-size`, `--vacuum-time`) from destructive shortcuts (`rm -rf`, disabling the daemon)
realWorldValue: EX200 Skill 4.1.7 and 4.1.8 test the ability to locate, interpret, and preserve system journals. In production, enabling persistent journals is a one-line change (`mkdir /var/log/journal`) that every new host should have — without it, evidence disappears on every reboot just when you need it most.

title: Archive and Restore Files with tar on RHEL 10
description: Type each tar command to create a compressed archive of /etc, list its contents, and extract it to a staging directory. Flags can appear in any order and combined short flags are accepted.
scenario: You need a throwaway backup of `/etc` before testing a risky config change. Create the archive at `/tmp/etc-backup.tar.gz`, confirm its contents by listing them, and extract the archive to `/tmp/restore` to prove you could roll back. Flags can appear in any order; combined short flags like `-czf` are accepted. Use `tar --help` to explore options.

steps.task: Create a gzip-compressed archive at `/tmp/etc-backup.tar.gz` containing `/etc`.
steps.hint: Three flags: one to create, one to request gzip compression, and one that takes the output file as its value. Then the path to archive.

requirements.description: -c, --create                   create a new archive
-z, --gzip                     filter the archive through gzip
-f, --file=FILE                use archive file FILE
<path>                         path to include in the archive

distractors.description: -v, --verbose                  verbosely list files processed
-j, --bzip2                    filter the archive through bzip2 (wrong format for this task)
-p, --preserve-permissions     preserve permissions on extract (no effect when creating)

steps.successOutput: tar: Removing leading `/' from member names

steps.task: List the contents of `/tmp/etc-backup.tar.gz` without extracting anything.
steps.hint: Swap the create flag for the list flag. Compression and file flags stay the same.

requirements.description: -t, --list                     list the contents of an archive
-z, --gzip                     filter the archive through gzip
-f, --file=FILE                use archive file FILE

distractors.description: -v, --verbose                  verbosely list files processed
-W, --verify                   attempt to verify the archive after writing (creation only)
--strip-components=N           strip N leading components from file names on extract

steps.task: Extract `/tmp/etc-backup.tar.gz` into `/tmp/restore` (assume the directory already exists).
steps.hint: Four flags this time: extract, gzip, file (with value), and change-directory (with value).

requirements.description: -x, --extract                  extract files from an archive
-z, --gzip                     filter the archive through gzip
-f, --file=FILE                use archive file FILE
-C, --directory=DIR            change to directory DIR before extracting

distractors.description: --overwrite                    overwrite existing files on extract
-k, --keep-old-files           do not overwrite existing files (opposite of --overwrite)
--strip-components=N           strip N leading components from file names on extract

explanation:
`tar` is the workhorse archiver on RHEL and its flag vocabulary follows a consistent grammar.

**Three action flags, pick one per invocation:**
- `-c` create an archive
- `-t` list contents without extracting
- `-x` extract from an archive

**Two flags that stay constant in this lab:**
- `-z` tells tar to filter through `gzip`. Required whether you are creating, listing, or extracting a `.tar.gz`.
- `-f FILE` names the archive. On RHEL the value immediately follows `-f`, which is why combined short flags like `-czf archive.tar.gz` work: `f` is always the last letter so the value binds to it.

**Extract-only flag:**
- `-C DIR` changes directory before extracting. Without it, files land relative to your current working directory — a common cause of "tarbomb" messes in `/tmp` or `/root`.

**Distractors worth knowing anyway:**
- `-j` filters through bzip2 (wrong compression for a `.tar.gz`).
- `-v` adds verbose output — helpful at the terminal, unnecessary in scripts.
- `--strip-components=N` is useful when restoring paths captured from `/` back into a relative directory, but is not needed here.

**Flag order does not matter.** `tar -czf file /etc`, `tar --create --gzip --file=file /etc`, and `tar /etc -czf file` are all accepted. What does matter is that `-f` is followed by the archive filename (or uses the `--file=NAME` long form).
learningOutcomes: Create, list, and extract gzip-compressed tar archives using `tar -c`, `-t`, and `-x`
Combine short flags (`-czf`) and use long forms (`--create`, `--gzip`, `--file=`)
Extract safely into a specific directory with `-C` to avoid cluttering the working directory
realWorldValue: EX200 Skill 1.1.6 tests tar directly, and every RHEL admin uses tar weekly — for backups, config snapshots, software distribution, and shipping evidence to support. Knowing the three-letter grammar `-c/-t/-x` + `-z` + `-f` from memory is essential under exam time pressure.

title: Configure firewalld Zones and Services on RHEL 10
description: Type each firewall-cmd invocation to set the default zone, permanently add a service, and reload the runtime configuration. Flags can appear in any order. Use --help to explore the firewall-cmd vocabulary.
scenario: A RHEL 10 edge host needs its default zone set to `public`, HTTP traffic permitted persistently in that zone, and the runtime config reloaded so the new rule takes effect. Flags can appear in any order. Use `firewall-cmd --help` to explore options — several distractors look relevant but are wrong for this task.

steps.task: Set the firewalld default zone to `public` (this change takes effect immediately and is persistent, no --permanent needed).
steps.hint: A single flag-value pair. Watch out for the read-only variant that only reports the current default.

requirements.description: --set-default-zone=ZONE        set the default zone (persistent, no reload required)

distractors.description: --get-default-zone             print the current default zone (read-only)
--zone=ZONE                    target a specific zone for another operation (not for changing the default)
--add-source=SOURCE            bind a source address to a zone

steps.task: Permanently allow the `http` service in the `public` zone.
steps.hint: Three arguments together: which zone, which service to add, and the permanent flag so the rule survives a reload or reboot.

requirements.description: --zone=ZONE                    operate on the specified zone
--add-service=SERVICE          add a service to the zone
--permanent                    make the change persist across reloads/reboots

distractors.description: --add-port=PORT/PROTO          add a raw port (wrong flag when a named service already exists)
--add-interface=INTERFACE      bind a network interface to the zone (not required here)
--runtime-to-permanent         promote all current runtime rules to permanent (too broad for one rule)
--remove-service=SERVICE       remove a service from the zone (opposite of add)

steps.task: Reload firewalld so the permanent rule you just added is applied to the running configuration.
steps.hint: A single flag. One distractor drops all runtime connections, another only reports state — neither is what you want.

requirements.description: --reload                       reload firewall rules, keeping state information

distractors.description: --complete-reload              reload firewall rules, losing state (drops established connections)
--runtime-to-permanent         save current runtime rules as permanent (opposite direction to what is needed)
--state                        return the running state of firewalld (read-only)

explanation:
firewalld uses a *runtime* and a *permanent* configuration which are normally separate. The flag vocabulary is dense and easy to mistake.

**Step 1: `firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=public`**
- `--set-default-zone` changes `/etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf` and also applies immediately — it is the exception that does **not** need `--permanent` or a reload.
- Distractor: `--get-default-zone` only reads, it does not write.
- Distractor: `--zone=public` alone does nothing; it only scopes another operation to that zone.

**Step 2: `firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent`**
- `--zone=public` targets a specific zone instead of the default.
- `--add-service=http` references a named service defined in `/usr/lib/firewalld/services/`. Prefer named services over raw ports (`--add-port=80/tcp`) when one exists — they cover every port the service uses and read better in audits.
- `--permanent` writes to `/etc/firewalld/zones/public.xml`. Without it, the rule exists only in runtime and disappears at the next reload or reboot.
- Distractor: `--runtime-to-permanent` promotes *every* current runtime rule to permanent, which is a sledgehammer when you just want this one change saved.

**Step 3: `firewall-cmd --reload`**
- `--reload` re-reads the permanent config into the runtime, applying the new rule while **preserving established connections** tracked by conntrack.
- Distractor: `--complete-reload` also works but drops connection state — valid for major rule changes, overkill for adding one service.
- Distractor: `--state` only reports whether firewalld is running.

**Flag order does not matter** — `--permanent --zone=public --add-service=http` is just as valid. What matters is that every permanent change is followed by `--reload` before it affects traffic.
learningOutcomes: Change the firewalld default zone with `--set-default-zone` (no `--permanent` needed)
Permanently add a named service to a specific zone with `--zone`, `--add-service`, and `--permanent`
Know when to use `--reload` vs `--complete-reload`, and recognise read-only flags like `--state` and `--get-default-zone`
realWorldValue: EX200 Skill 10.1.1 tests firewalld directly. The number-one mistake under exam pressure is forgetting `--permanent`, reloading, and then watching the rule vanish. Knowing the permanent / runtime / reload triangle — and which flags bypass it — is what separates a quick pass from a slow fail.

title: Sequence the RHEL 10 Boot Process
description: Drag the stages of a RHEL 10 boot into the correct order, from firmware power-on through systemd activating the default target and a login prompt appearing.
scenario: You are explaining the RHEL 10 boot sequence to a new hire. Drag each stage into the correct position, starting from firmware power-on and finishing at an interactive login prompt.

steps.text: UEFI firmware completes POST and loads the EFI boot entry from the ESP
The GRUB2 boot loader is loaded and displays the menu of bootable kernels
GRUB2 loads the selected kernel (`vmlinuz`) and `initramfs` into memory and hands off
The kernel mounts `initramfs` as a temporary root and probes hardware/modules
`systemd` is started as PID 1 from `initramfs`
systemd pivots to the real root filesystem on disk
systemd activates the default target (`multi-user.target` or `graphical.target`)
`getty`/`gdm` starts and presents a login prompt on the console

explanation:
A RHEL 10 boot is a chain where each stage hands control to the next. Skipping a step is not possible — every stage produces the state the next one needs.

1. **Firmware** — UEFI completes POST (Power On Self Test) and reads its boot entry list. The default entry on RHEL 10 points at `\EFI\redhat\shimx64.efi` on the EFI System Partition.
2. **GRUB2** — the shim chains into GRUB2, which reads `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` and presents the kernel menu. On EX200 this is where you press `e` to edit a boot entry for single-user recovery.
3. **Kernel + initramfs load** — GRUB2 loads the selected `vmlinuz` kernel and the `initramfs` archive into memory, then jumps into the kernel.
4. **Kernel bring-up** — the kernel decompresses, mounts the `initramfs` as a temporary root filesystem, and probes hardware to load the modules it needs (including storage drivers).
5. **systemd (initramfs)** — `systemd` starts as PID 1 inside the `initramfs`. This is the earliest point at which unit files run.
6. **Pivot to real root** — once the real root filesystem is accessible (RAID/LVM/encrypted volumes sorted), systemd pivots onto it and discards the `initramfs`.
7. **Default target** — systemd activates `default.target`, which is a symlink to `multi-user.target` or `graphical.target`. Use `systemctl get-default` to see which.
8. **Login prompt** — once the target's dependencies are reached, `getty` or `gdm` opens a login on the TTY or display.
learningOutcomes: Recall the order of RHEL 10 boot stages from firmware to login prompt
Identify the boundary where each stage hands off (firmware → GRUB → kernel → systemd)
Know where to intervene to recover a broken boot (GRUB menu, `rd.break`, `systemctl default`)
realWorldValue: Boot failures are the scariest tickets on a RHEL host because the usual remote-troubleshooting tools are not available yet. Knowing where each stage lives, and which handoff is failing, is the difference between 'hung at GRUB' and 'hung in initramfs' — and determines whether you drop into GRUB edit mode, an emergency shell, or boot into a different target.

title: Match RHEL Text Tool Flags to Their Behaviour
description: Drag each `find`, `grep`, and `sed` flag or pattern to the behaviour it produces. Covers the core EX200 text-processing vocabulary you reach for under time pressure.
scenario: You are triaging a RHEL 10 host and juggling `find`, `grep`, and `sed`. Match each flag or pattern on the left to the behaviour it produces on the right.

pairs.definition: Match only regular files (not directories, symlinks, or sockets)
Match files last modified more than seven 24-hour periods ago
Search recursively, descending into every subdirectory under `/etc`
Invert the match — print only lines that do NOT contain the pattern
Treat the pattern as an extended regular expression (alternation, `+`, `?`)
Edit the file in place, replacing every occurrence of `old` with `new` on each line
Suppress default output and print only lines 5 through 10
Print the third whitespace-separated field of each line

explanation:
RHCSA rewards fluency with the Unix text triplet. A few shortcuts that always come up:

- **`find -type f`** — filter by inode type. `d` for directories, `l` for symlinks, `s` for sockets. Combine with `-name`, `-mtime`, `-size` to narrow further.
- **`find -mtime +N`** — the plus means *more than* N days. `-mtime -N` is *within* N days, `-mtime N` is *exactly* N.
- **`grep -r`** — recurses into subdirectories, following the directory tree. Pair with `--include='*.conf'` to scope to a file pattern.
- **`grep -v`** — the invert-match flag. Critical for log triage: `grep -v INFO /var/log/messages` drops the noise.
- **`grep -E`** — extended regex unlocks `|`, `+`, `?` without needing to backslash them. `grep -F` turns the pattern into fixed strings (fastest, safest for literals).
- **`sed -i`** — in-place edit. Always combine with a backup (`sed -i.bak`) during the exam so you have an escape hatch.
- **`sed -n 'RANGEp'`** — the `-n` suppresses default auto-print, so only the explicitly `p`rinted lines appear.
- **`awk '{print $N}'`** — `awk` splits on whitespace (or `-F:` for a custom delimiter like `/etc/passwd`). `$0` is the whole line.
learningOutcomes: Know the common `find` predicates: `-type`, `-mtime`, `-name`, `-size`
Recall the meaning of core `grep` flags: `-r`, `-v`, `-E`, `-F`, `-i`
Use `sed -i` safely for in-place edits and `awk '{print $N}'` for field extraction
realWorldValue: EX200 Skill 1.1.3 tests `grep` and regex directly, and Skill 1.1.11 expects you to navigate `/usr/share/doc` and man pages. But in practice, the whole exam is gated on your speed with `find | xargs grep | sed`. Every minute you save not re-reading `man find` is a minute you get back to answer a harder question.

title: Fill in the dnf, rpm, and subscription-manager Commands
description: Complete each package-management invocation by filling in the missing subcommand or flag. Covers the `dnf`, `rpm`, and `subscription-manager` patterns every RHEL admin runs daily.
scenario: You are setting up a fresh RHEL 10 host: register it, install and update packages, and identify where files come from. Fill in the blanks to complete each command.

questions.hint: The subcommand that attaches this host to Red Hat's Content Delivery Network.
The one-character flag that answers 'yes' to every confirmation prompt.
The subcommand that upgrades an already-installed package to the latest available version.
Combined short flags: query mode plus 'find which package owns this file'.
The subcommand that enumerates packages; `--installed` narrows the listing to only those currently present.
Not `update` — the subcommand that shows the audit trail of dnf transactions and supports rollback.

explanation:
Package management on RHEL 10 spans three tools that work together.

**`subscription-manager`** connects the host to Red Hat's Content Delivery Network. Without `register`, `dnf` has no repositories for the base OS. `subscription-manager repos --list` then enables/disables channels.

**`dnf`** is the high-level package manager. Core subcommands:
- `install [-y]` — install packages (`-y` for unattended)
- `update` / `upgrade` — upgrade to newer versions; they are aliases on RHEL 10
- `remove` / `erase` — remove packages
- `list --installed` / `list --available` / `list --updates` — enumerate packages
- `search TERM` — search package metadata
- `history` — transaction audit log; `dnf history undo N` rolls one back
- `info PKG` — detailed metadata on a single package

**`rpm`** is the low-level backend. You rarely install with `rpm -i` on RHEL because `dnf` resolves dependencies. But `rpm -q*` is indispensable:
- `rpm -qa` — list all installed packages
- `rpm -qf PATH` — which package owns a file
- `rpm -ql PKG` — list files installed by a package
- `rpm -qi PKG` — info on an installed package
- `rpm -V PKG` — verify a package's files against the database

Combined short flags like `-qf`, `-ql`, `-qa` are the RHCSA norm — learn them as units, not as individual flags.
learningOutcomes: Register a host with Red Hat using `subscription-manager register`
Install, update, remove, and list packages with `dnf`
Identify file ownership and package contents with `rpm -qf` and `rpm -ql`
Audit and roll back transactions with `dnf history`
realWorldValue: EX200 Domain 2 and Skill 7.1.5 both test package management, and every troubleshooting question eventually comes back to 'which package owns this file?' (`rpm -qf`) or 'when did this change?' (`dnf history`). Fluency with these flags is the single highest-leverage RHCSA skill.

title: Fix a Broken Log-Cleanup Bash Script on RHEL 10
description: A nightly cron job that trims old application logs is silently failing. Edit the bash script to make it correct, safe, and returning meaningful exit codes.
scenario: A cron job on a RHEL 10 host runs `/usr/local/sbin/cleanup-logs.sh` every night to remove `.log` files in `/var/log/app` older than 30 days. It has been failing silently for weeks. Fix the script so it runs cleanly, handles a missing directory, and returns a non-zero exit code on failure.
brokenCode:
LOG_DIR=/var/log/app
DAYS=30

if [ -d $LOG_DIR ]
    find $LOG_DIR -name *.log -mtime +$DAYS -exec rm {}
    exit 0
fi
correctCode:
#!/bin/bash
LOG_DIR=/var/log/app
DAYS=30

if [ -d "$LOG_DIR" ]; then
    find "$LOG_DIR" -name "*.log" -mtime +"$DAYS" -exec rm {} \;
    exit 0
else
    echo "Log directory $LOG_DIR not found" >&2
    exit 1
fi
explanation:
The broken script has five separate bugs, any one of which would mask the others on a cron run.

**1. Missing shebang**. cron hands the file to `/bin/sh`, which on RHEL is `bash` in POSIX mode — most of the time this works, but glob behaviour and `[[` availability differ. Adding `#!/bin/bash` makes the intended interpreter explicit.

**2. Missing `then`**. `if [ -d $LOG_DIR ]` must be followed by `then` on the next line or `; then` on the same line. Without it, bash emits a syntax error and cron silently swallows it.

**3. Unquoted variable `$LOG_DIR`**. If the variable is ever empty (say, someone comments out the assignment), `[ -d ]` evaluates differently than `[ -d "" ]`. Always quote path variables in tests.

**4. Unquoted glob `*.log`**. Bash expands `*.log` against the current working directory *before* passing it to `find`. If there are no `.log` files in CWD, `find` gets the literal `*.log` and it happens to work; if there are, `find` receives whatever matched in CWD instead. Quote the pattern so `find` does the globbing itself.

**5. Missing `-exec` terminator**. `-exec COMMAND \;` (or `\+`) is how `find` knows where the command ends. Without the terminator, `find` errors out with `find: missing argument to \`-exec'`.

**6. No else branch, no failure exit code**. If `$LOG_DIR` does not exist, the script silently succeeds — cron will happily continue calling it forever and you never learn the directory went away. The fix logs the failure to stderr and exits non-zero so cron's mail-on-error wakes someone up.
learningOutcomes: Write bash scripts with correct `if/then/else/fi` structure
Always quote path variables and glob patterns passed to `find`
Terminate `find -exec COMMAND` with `\;` or `\+`
Exit non-zero on failure so cron surfaces the problem instead of swallowing it
realWorldValue: EX200 Domain 3 tests shell scripting fundamentals and Skill 7.1.1 covers cron. In production, the most dangerous cleanup scripts are the ones that *silently succeed* — they delete the wrong thing, or they stop running, and nobody notices until the disk is full or data is missing. Noisy failure is always safer than silent success.

title: Harden /etc/ssh/sshd_config on RHEL 10
description: Walk through the stock RHEL 10 sshd_config and flip each directive to its hardened value. Covers password/key policy, session timeouts, and user allowlisting.
scenario: A RHEL 10 host will be exposed to the internet. Harden `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` by changing each directive from its stock value to the hardened value used in the CIS RHEL 10 benchmark.
explanation:
The RHEL 10 defaults in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` are tuned for compatibility, not hardening. Seven changes take an internet-exposed host from 'vulnerable to credential stuffing' to 'CIS-compliant'.

- **`PasswordAuthentication no`** — require public keys. Must come after you have verified key auth works, per the cutover pattern from the SSH key-based auth lab.
- **`PermitRootLogin no`** — never allow direct root login over SSH. `prohibit-password` is the middle ground (keys only for root), but `no` is safer for RHCSA and CIS.
- **`PubkeyAuthentication yes`** — the stock value is already `yes`, but this config intentionally has it flipped off to confirm you know to turn it on.
- **`MaxAuthTries 3`** — the default `6` is generous. Three tries per session is the CIS recommendation and slows online brute-force.
- **`ClientAliveInterval 300`** — the default `0` disables idle detection. 300 seconds (5 minutes) combined with the default `ClientAliveCountMax 3` kicks idle sessions after 15 minutes, limiting unattended exposure.
- **`X11Forwarding no`** — server-side X11 tunnelling is a pointless attack surface on a production RHEL host. Turn it off unless you have a concrete desktop-over-SSH use case.
- **`PermitEmptyPasswords no`** — already the default, but included because misconfigurations elsewhere (PAM, `/etc/shadow`) can create empty-password accounts. Double insurance.

After editing, always run `sshd -t` to syntax-check and then `systemctl reload sshd` (not restart — reload preserves existing sessions).
learningOutcomes: Identify the RHEL 10 stock `sshd_config` values and know which are unsafe
Map each directive to a threat it mitigates (password brute-force, session hijack, X11 abuse)
Know the order: edit → `sshd -t` → `systemctl reload sshd`
realWorldValue: Every RHEL host exposed to the internet is attacked within minutes of coming online. Default SSH settings are the most common vector. EX200 Skill 10.1.3 tests key-based auth directly, but grading rubrics also expect a hardened `sshd_config` — leaving password auth on loses marks even if the keys work.

title: Choose the Correct SELinux Remediation on RHEL 10
description: For each SELinux scenario (wrong context, unlabelled port, blocked boolean, stale labels after restore) pick the correct remediation from the RHCSA toolkit. Wrong answers include common exam traps.
scenario: A RHEL 10 host is in Enforcing mode. Four separate services are failing because of SELinux. For each resource, pick the *correct* remediation. Several wrong options are plausible-looking shortcuts that graders and auditors will reject.

issues.issue: httpd logs `AH00132: file permissions deny server access` and the files show `unconfined_u:object_r:var_t:s0` contexts instead of `httpd_sys_content_t`.
options: Run `chmod -R 777 /srv/web` to bypass the permission error

issues.resource: httpd reconfigured to listen on port 8080
issues.issue: `systemctl start httpd` fails with `(13)Permission denied: AH00072: make_sock: could not bind to address [::]:8080`. AVC denial shows httpd_t blocked from binding to an unlabelled port.
options: Run `setenforce 0` so httpd can bind to any port

issues.resource: Users reporting that CGI scripts in their ~/public_html directories are refused
issues.issue: Apache logs show SELinux AVC denials on httpd_t accessing user home directories. The fix must persist across reboots.

issues.resource: A directory tree restored from backup into /var/www
issues.issue: Many files now carry stale or incorrect SELinux contexts (user_home_t, default_t). You need to re-apply the contexts defined by the current policy without hand-editing each file.
options: Run `setenforce 0` and leave the contexts as-is

explanation:
SELinux remediation on RHEL comes down to four tools. Knowing which one applies is the whole skill.

**1. File context (`semanage fcontext` + `restorecon`)** — when a file is in the wrong place or a new path exists outside the default policy. `semanage fcontext -a` registers the mapping persistently; `restorecon` applies it to files on disk. Always run them as a pair — one without the other is half the fix.

**2. Port labels (`semanage port`)** — when a service needs to bind to a non-default port. Without the label, SELinux denies the bind regardless of firewall rules, because `httpd_t` is only permitted to bind to ports tagged `http_port_t`.

**3. Booleans (`setsebool -P`)** — when policy already anticipates the scenario but has it switched off by default. The `-P` is critical: without it the change reverts on reboot. Common booleans for RHCSA: `httpd_enable_homedirs`, `httpd_can_network_connect`, `ftp_home_dir`, `samba_enable_home_dirs`.

**4. `restorecon`** — when contexts have been corrupted by copying, restoring, or `chcon` (which does not update the policy database). `restorecon -Rv PATH` re-applies what the *policy* says the path should be, overwriting whatever drift got in.

**Why the wrong answers are traps:**
- `setenforce 0` hides the problem but leaves the policy misaligned. Auditors see it immediately, and a reboot re-enables enforcement — leading to a 'works on my machine' regression.
- `chmod 777` answers a DAC permission question, not a MAC (SELinux) question. SELinux denials have nothing to do with Unix modes.
- `chcon` changes the on-disk context *without* updating the policy database, so the next `restorecon` silently reverts it. Almost never the right answer for persistent fixes.
- Disabling firewalld or changing ports are wrong-scope fixes that avoid the SELinux lesson.
learningOutcomes: Diagnose SELinux failures by distinguishing file context, port label, and boolean issues
Apply the correct remediation: `semanage fcontext`+`restorecon`, `semanage port`, `setsebool -P`, `restorecon`
Recognise `setenforce 0`, `chmod 777`, and `chcon` (for persistence) as exam traps
realWorldValue: Every RHCSA SELinux question is really 'pick the right tool'. Getting this right in practice means the difference between a clean audit and a deduction; in production, it is the difference between a secure host and one where someone has silently been running Permissive for three years because 'SELinux was blocking things'.

title: Fix a Broken /etc/sudoers.d Snippet on RHEL 10
description: Edit a broken sudoers drop-in so the developers group can manage httpd without a password, while keeping the `webdev` user's scope narrow. Mind the syntax — a bad sudoers file breaks sudo for everyone.
scenario: A junior admin has left `/etc/sudoers.d/developers` in a broken state. The `developers` group should be able to restart, reload, and query status of `httpd` without a password, and the user `webdev` should be able to run `dnf update` (only dnf update, nothing else). Fix the file so it is syntactically valid and scoped correctly.
brokenPolicy:
# Allow developers group to manage httpd
%developers ALL = /bin/systemctl restart httpd, NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl status httpd
webdev ALL=(ALL) ALL
correctPolicy:
# Allow developers group to manage httpd
%developers ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart httpd, /bin/systemctl reload httpd, /bin/systemctl status httpd
webdev ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/dnf update
explanation:
The broken file has three separate defects, all of which are common RHCSA traps.

**1. Missing runas specification.** `%developers ALL = /bin/systemctl ...` omits the `(root)` runas. `sudoers` syntax is `user HOST=(RUNAS) COMMANDS`. Without `(RUNAS)`, sudo has to fall back to defaults and `visudo` will usually reject the line outright as a syntax error.

**2. Misplaced `NOPASSWD`.** `NOPASSWD:` is a tag that applies to the command that follows — and only until the next tag or end of line. In the broken line, `restart httpd` requires a password but `status httpd` does not, which is the opposite of the intent. The fix places `NOPASSWD:` *before all* the commands so it applies to each.

**3. Over-broad grant to `webdev`.** `webdev ALL=(ALL) ALL` means 'webdev can run anything, as anyone, anywhere'. That is the same as giving webdev root. The intent was to allow only `dnf update`, so the fix is `webdev ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/dnf update`.

**General sudoers rules for RHCSA:**
- Edit with `visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/FILE` — it syntax-checks before saving and refuses to save a broken file (which would lock everyone out of sudo).
- Drop-in files under `/etc/sudoers.d/` are included automatically. Filenames must not contain dots or tildes (they are skipped silently).
- Always use full absolute command paths (`/bin/systemctl`, not `systemctl`) — a relative path lets the user satisfy the rule with a binary they placed in `$PATH`.
- `%groupname` refers to a Unix group; plain `username` is a single user.
learningOutcomes: Write correct sudoers syntax: `user HOST=(RUNAS) [TAG:] COMMANDS`
Place `NOPASSWD:` so it applies to every command that should be passwordless
Grant narrow, absolute-path commands instead of `(ALL) ALL`
Use `visudo -f` to edit drop-in files safely
realWorldValue: EX200 Skill 9.1.4 tests privileged access, and sudoers is the tool that implements it. A mistake here is one of the few RHCSA mistakes that can lock you out of root — making this exactly the kind of place the exam (and post-incident reviews) pay close attention.

title: Diagnose a Failed httpd Start from journald on RHEL 10
description: Read the journald output for a failed `httpd.service` start and identify the root cause. Covers systemd log prefixes, start-limit-hit behaviour, and distinguishing signal from noise.
scenario: A RHEL 10 host's `httpd.service` will not start after a certificate rotation. The on-call engineer has captured the last two minutes of journald output (`journalctl -u httpd -b -n 40`). Read the logs and identify the true root cause.

logs.message: Starting The Apache HTTP Server...
AH00526: Syntax error on line 42 of /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf:
SSLCertificateFile: file '/etc/pki/tls/certs/wildcard-prod.pem' does not exist or is empty
httpd.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
httpd.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
Failed to start The Apache HTTP Server.
httpd.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1.
Stopped The Apache HTTP Server.
Starting The Apache HTTP Server...
AH00526: Syntax error on line 42 of /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf:
SSLCertificateFile: file '/etc/pki/tls/certs/wildcard-prod.pem' does not exist or is empty
httpd.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
httpd.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 5.
httpd.service: Start request repeated too quickly.
httpd.service: Failed with result 'start-limit-hit'.
Failed to start The Apache HTTP Server.

answers.text: httpd was OOM-killed by the kernel — the host is out of memory
The SSL configuration on line 42 of ssl.conf references `/etc/pki/tls/certs/wildcard-prod.pem`, which is missing or empty
SELinux is blocking httpd from binding to port 443 — run `setenforce 0` to confirm
Another process is already listening on port 80 — investigate with `ss -tlnp`
systemd hit its start-limit, which means httpd was otherwise healthy but simply restarted too often — clear with `systemctl reset-failed`

explanation:
Reading systemd journals is an exercise in separating the *root cause* line from the *consequence* lines.

**The signal**: `SSLCertificateFile: file '/etc/pki/tls/certs/wildcard-prod.pem' does not exist or is empty`. This is httpd telling you exactly what is missing — a certificate rotation that did not complete. Everything else is downstream.

**The noise that trips people up**:
- `httpd.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'` — systemd reporting the service exited non-zero. This is a *consequence*, not a cause.
- `httpd.service: Start request repeated too quickly` / `'start-limit-hit'` — systemd giving up after 5 failed restarts within its default window. This is also a consequence; running `systemctl reset-failed` only clears the flag so you can try again — it does not fix the underlying missing cert.
- `Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 5` — shows systemd's auto-restart behaviour kicking in (driven by `Restart=on-failure` in the unit). It is the symptom, not the problem.

**The wrong answers**:
- *OOM* — no `Out of memory` messages from the kernel, no oom-killer line. Eliminated.
- *SELinux* — no AVC denials present. `setenforce 0` is the reflex wrong answer on RHCSA.
- *Port conflict* — httpd is exiting *before* it reaches the bind step; the error is in config parsing, not sockets.
- *start-limit-hit as root cause* — tempting because it is the last thing in the log, but it is the *effect* of repeated failures, not the cause.

**The fix** is to restore or re-issue the certificate at the path referenced by `ssl.conf`, verify with `httpd -t`, then `systemctl reset-failed httpd && systemctl start httpd`.
learningOutcomes: Read a journald excerpt and separate root-cause messages from consequence messages
Recognise `start-limit-hit` as a systemd rate-limit symptom, not a root cause
Understand that `reset-failed` clears state but does not fix the underlying problem
Confirm a configuration fix with `httpd -t` before restarting the service
realWorldValue: EX200 Skill 4.1.7 tests interpreting system logs and journals. The harder skill — which the exam also probes — is picking the *right* line out of a noisy journal. Candidates who reach for `setenforce 0` or `reset-failed` as the first move lose marks and, in production, hide bugs instead of fixing them.

title: Triage a Disk-Full + OOM Incident on a RHEL 10 Host
description: A production RHEL 10 host is in crisis: / is 99% full, journald is ballooning, httpd is failing, and the OOM killer has just taken mysqld. Triage across alerts, metrics, logs, and timeline, then choose only the correct remediation actions.
scenario: At 14:30 UTC, PagerDuty fires for `web-prod-07`. The on-call receives a disk-full alert, then an OOM-killed process alert within 8 minutes. Triage by cross-referencing alerts, metrics, logs, and the event timeline, then pick only the correct response actions and identify the true root cause.

alerts.message: httpd.service failed: journald refuses writes (disk full)
Low memory condition on web-prod-07 (available < 256 MB)
Out of memory: Killed process 2104 (mysqld), reaped 1.2 GB

logs.message: Failed to write entry (15 items, 1024 bytes) despite vacuuming, ignoring: No space left on device
(28)No space left on device: AH00099: could not create /var/log/httpd/error_log
systemd-journald invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x100cca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE), order=0
Out of memory: Killed process 2104 (mysqld) total-vm:1824MB, anon-rss:1210MB
InnoDB: Operating system error number 28 in a file operation. (ENOSPC)

timeline.event: Host healthy. Baseline metrics within normal range.
Nightly backup cron starts writing to /var/backups (on the / partition).
Backup growth pushes / past 90% — pre-alarm logged to journald.
systemd-journald can no longer write; httpd fails its first log rotation.
Journald buffers in memory, driving available memory below 256 MB.
Kernel invokes OOM killer; mysqld (the largest resident process) is killed.

actions.description: Identify the largest consumers on / with `du -xh / | sort -rh | head -30`
Cap journald size with `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` to free space immediately
Move `/var/backups` to a separate filesystem once / has breathing room
Run `setenforce 0` to rule out SELinux as the cause
Reboot the host immediately to clear the OOM state
Delete `/var/log/journal` entirely with `rm -rf` to free space
Set a persistent journal size cap in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` (SystemMaxUse=1G)
Kill all processes with `killall -9` to free memory

answers.text: DDoS attack filled httpd logs, which cascaded into disk-full and then OOM
Backup-to-/ + unbounded journald filled the disk; journald buffering then consumed RAM and triggered OOM against mysqld
mysqld had a memory leak that drove the host out of memory; the disk alert is unrelated
A kernel bug caused systemd-journald to corrupt the filesystem

explanation:
The story the data tells, when you line up the four panels, is one cascading failure with two independent contributors.

**Contributor 1 — unbounded `/var/backups` on /.** The timeline shows the nightly backup starting at 14:02 UTC, and the disk-usage metric climbs from 85% at 14:00 to 99% by 14:30. Backups sharing the same filesystem as `/var/log` and `/var/lib/mysql` is the real design flaw.

**Contributor 2 — no cap on journald.** The journal metric more than doubles between 14:20 and 14:30 (2.2 GB → 3.8 GB). Default RHEL 10 journald has `SystemMaxUse=` unset, meaning it uses up to 10% of the filesystem. As the filesystem fills, that 10% cap becomes a moving target, and on a nearly-full `/` there is no headroom left for it to vacuum into.

**Why the OOM.** When journald cannot write to disk (ENOSPC), it buffers pending journal entries in memory. On a busy host this buffer grows fast. Between 14:20 and 14:30 the available-memory series drops from 800 MB to 80 MB — that 720 MB loss is almost exactly the journal growth over the same window. The OOM killer targets the largest RSS process; mysqld at 1.2 GB wins that lottery.

**Correct actions, in order:**
1. `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` — this is the fastest reversible free-disk move. Buys you breathing room without destroying logs wholesale.
2. `du -xh / | sort -rh | head` — identify the largest contributors; confirms `/var/backups` as the primary culprit.
3. Move `/var/backups` to a separate filesystem (or a remote destination) so future backups cannot fill `/`.
4. Set `SystemMaxUse=1G` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and `systemctl restart systemd-journald` so journald caps itself persistently.

**Wrong actions and why:**
- `setenforce 0` — there are no AVC denials. Classic reflexive wrong answer.
- Reboot — clears the OOM flag but the disk is still 99% full; the cycle repeats immediately.
- `rm -rf /var/log/journal` — destroys *all* persistent journals, including the evidence you need for the post-incident review. Use vacuum with a bound instead.
- `killall -9` — kills unrelated processes and does not address the root cause.
learningOutcomes: Cross-reference alerts, metrics, logs, and timeline to build a coherent incident narrative
Diagnose disk-full + OOM cascades where journald buffering is the link between them
Choose reversible, bounded remediations (vacuum-size, SystemMaxUse) over destructive shortcuts (rm -rf, reboot)
Apply durable fixes (move backups off /, cap journald in journald.conf) once the immediate crisis is clear
realWorldValue: This incident pattern — unbounded logs on the same filesystem as application data, combined with no journald cap — has caused countless production outages on RHEL hosts. EX200 tests the individual tools (`journalctl`, `du`, `systemctl`), but the senior-admin skill is reading a dashboard and choosing the correct sequence under pressure without making the outage worse.

title: Configure autofs for On-Demand NFS Home Directories
description: Build the correct command sequence to configure autofs on a RHEL 10 client so user home directories mount on demand from an NFS server. Exclude destructive distractors that would break NFS or remove the mapping.
scenario: A RHEL 10 workstation needs on-demand NFS home directories from `nfs.example.com:/export/home/` mounted under `/home/<user>` via autofs. Drag the correct commands into the queue in the right order. Three of the listed commands are distractors that would disable NFS or erase the mapping.

commands.errorOutput: autofs and nfs-utils must be installed first; every later step depends on the `automount` daemon and NFS client tooling.
Install autofs first so `/etc/auto.master` exists as part of the autofs package.
Install autofs first — the auto.master reference needs a real auto.home map to point at.
Configure both auto.master and auto.home before starting autofs, otherwise the daemon starts with no mappings.
autofs must be running before an access to `/home/webdev` will trigger an automount.
You need to have triggered the automount (by accessing a home directory) before `mount` shows it.
DISTRACTOR: Disabling `nfs-client.target` breaks every NFS mount on the host, including the one you are trying to configure. Never disable it as part of an NFS workflow.
DISTRACTOR: Blanking `/etc/auto.home` removes every mapping. autofs will start cleanly but no home directories will mount.
DISTRACTOR: A static `mount` bypasses autofs entirely, mounts the whole parent export over `/home`, and persists only until reboot. It is the opposite of on-demand per-user mounts.

explanation:
autofs on RHEL 10 is a two-file configuration that follows a strict pattern.

**Master map (`/etc/auto.master`)**: maps a directory prefix to an indirect map file. `/home /etc/auto.home` means 'whenever something under `/home/` is accessed, look it up in `/etc/auto.home`'.

**Indirect map (`/etc/auto.home`)**: maps a key (the part after `/home/`) to a mount source. The magic `*` key matches any username, and `&` in the source expands to whatever matched. So `* -rw,soft,intr nfs.example.com:/export/home/&` means: for any `/home/USER` access, mount `nfs.example.com:/export/home/USER` there with those options.

**Ordering rules**:
1. Install the packages first — `/etc/auto.master` is shipped by autofs and does not exist before install.
2. Edit both maps *before* starting the service. Starting it against empty maps just activates an empty daemon and masks the configuration error.
3. Only then `systemctl enable --now autofs`.
4. Accessing any `/home/USER` triggers the mount — the mount happens lazily, which is the whole point of autofs.

**Distractors to avoid:**
- `systemctl disable nfs-client.target` — tears down the entire NFS client stack; autofs can't mount NFS without it.
- `echo '' > /etc/auto.home` — wipes the map. autofs loads, finds no mappings, and no home directories mount.
